target_customer: Orthodontists and dental labs that want to design and print clear aligners in house instead of buying them from Invisalign
problem: Orthodontists paid about $1,700 per patient to Invisalign and lost patients to direct to consumer aligner startups, while 3D printers had become cheap enough to make aligners in the office.
business_model: Software licence charged per patient to orthodontists, later expanded to a factory made aligner service, printing materials and a practice dashboard
product_category: Orthodontic aligner design software and digital manufacturing

founders.name: Andrew Martz
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (2018-03-19) says he worked in his father's orthodontic office and saw that 3D printers had become capable enough for dental offices. YC page lists him as the only founder. Education and prior employers not found in opened sources.

competitors.name: Invisalign (Align Technology)
competitors.what: Market leading clear aligners sold through orthodontists
competitors.traction_then: Incumbent; orthodontists paid about $1,700 per patient according to ArchForm

competitors.name: SmileDirectClub
competitors.what: Direct to consumer aligners by mail
competitors.traction_then: Named as a direct to consumer rival; figures not given in the source

technical_complexity.rationale: Automated tooth segmentation, treatment planning and printable aligner geometry needed orthodontic software plus material and printer workflow, and later required FDA 510(k) clearance (K213916, December 2021).

defensibility.rationale: Software and workflow could be copied by dental CAD vendors; the regulatory clearance and later in house materials gave some protection but not at founding.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying or buying ArchForm; it was still operating in 2026 and sells a factory and direct print product.

market_need_then: Invisalign cost orthodontists about $1,700 per case against about $50 per patient quoted by ArchForm in March 2018, and direct to consumer aligner startups were pressuring practices (TechCrunch, 2018-03-19).

branding.domain_note: Uses archform.com; acquisition history not found

identity.visual_style: Clinical product marketing focused on savings and speed

brand_strength.rationale: Trade press coverage (TechCrunch, 3DPrint.com) exists but no sourced evidence of brand driven growth; the name is also a term for orthodontic wire shape, which crowds search results.

outcome_analysis: ArchForm rode falling 3D printer prices and orthodontist anger at Invisalign pricing, entering in 2018 with a per patient software fee far below the incumbent. It stayed independent, opened an in house aligner factory in 2020, filed a Form D in April 2020, won FDA 510(k) clearance in December 2021 and by 2026 claims millions of aligners made. Funding detail is thin so the scale of capital behind it is unclear.
notes: Funding unverified: aggregators (Caplight, The Company Check, CB Insights) report a roughly $7.8M to $8M total with a March 2020 round labelled seed by one and Series A by another, and a $120K seed in 2018; these were not confirmed by a primary source and are not recorded as rounds. Only the April 2020 Form D filing (amount not visible) is sourced. YC page says founded 2013, CB Insights says 2017; 2017 used. No acquisition or shutdown found.
